warmup.q: val buffer: MutableList<*> = mutableListOf("pay_1", "pay_2"). Which of these lines compiles?
options: buffer.add("pay_3"), because the list really holds strings
None of them: a star-projected list is read-only
warmup.why: Through MutableList<*> the compiler doesn't know the element type, so it refuses every call that passes an element in, even null (the unknown type might be non-nullable). clear() takes no element, so it compiles. A star projection limits which values go in; it does not make the list read-only.

sections.h: List<*> is a list of some type you don't know
sections.html:
A logging helper has to accept every list in the codebase: a List<String> of payment ids, a List<Int> of amounts, a List<Settlement>. It never needs to know the element type. Kotlin's way to say that is a star projection:

Java
static void logAll(List<?> items) {
    for (Object item : items) System.out.println("  " + item);   // each item is an Object
}

logAll(ids);      // List<String>
logAll(cents);    // List<Integer>
Kotlin
fun logAll(items: List<*>) {
    for (item in items) println("  $item")      // each item is Any?
}

logAll(ids)       // List<String>
logAll(cents)     // List<Int>

Read List<*> as "a list of some specific type, and I don't know which". The list really does have one element type. You've chosen not to name it. Java writes the same idea as List<?>, the unbounded wildcard.

What can you do with a list of an unknown type? Ask the same two questions as in the last lesson. Reading is safe, but all you know is that each element is something, so it comes out as Any?. Writing is not safe: the list might be a MutableList<Int>, so no String may go in. Kotlin doesn't even let null in, because the unknown type might be non-nullable:

star.add("pay_3")
Receiver type 'MutableList<*>' contains star projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'.

star.add(null)
Null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'CapturedType(*)'.

val id: String = star[0]
Initializer type mismatch: expected 'String', actual 'CapturedType(*)'.

Java is more relaxed about one of these. add(null) compiles on a List<?>, because every Java reference type allows null. add("pay_3") fails with String cannot be converted to CAP#1, the captured type from lesson 6.

Everything that doesn't take an element still works: size, isEmpty(), removeAt(0), clear(). So a function that empties any buffer can take a MutableList<*>. That's the drain function in this lesson's lab.

sections.h: What * stands for depends on how the parameter is declared
sections.html:
Take Source<out T : Number> first. A Source<*> might be a Source<Int> or a Source<BigDecimal>. Whichever it is, next() returns some Number, so Number is the most the compiler can promise. Now take Sink<in T>. A Sink<*> might be a Sink<String> or a Sink<CardAuthorized>. No value is accepted by every one of them, so the compiler allows none. Nothing is Kotlin's name for a type with no values, which is exactly that answer. Both answers come from the substitution question of lesson 4, asked about every type the star could stand for.

So a * is shorthand for the safest projection that the declaration allows, and what it means depends on the declared variance. The Kotlin docs write it as three rules:

  • For Source<out T : Number>, Source<*> means Source<out Number>. You can read, and reads keep the bound: you get a Number, not an Any?.
  • For Sink<in T>, Sink<*> means Sink<in Nothing>. No value has type Nothing, so you can't pass anything in at all.
  • For an invariant Box<T>, Box<*> means Box<out Any?> when you read and Box<in Nothing> when you write. (With a bound, Box<T : Payment>, reads would give Payment.)
Java
interface Source<T extends Number> { T next(); }
interface Sink<T> { void accept(T item); }

static Number peek(Source<?> source) { return source.next(); }   // the bound survives the ?

Sink<?> anySink = audit;
anySink.accept("pay_1");      // error: String cannot be converted to CAP#1
anySink.accept(null);         // compiles in Java
Kotlin
interface Source<out T : Number> { fun next(): T }
interface Sink<in T> { fun accept(item: T) }

fun peek(source: Source<*>): Number = source.next()   // the bound survives the *

val anySink: Sink<*> = audit
anySink.accept("pay_1")       // error: Receiver type 'Sink<*>' contains star projection which prohibits ...

The invariant case shows the Nothing plainly. Assign to the property of a Box<*> and the compiler says what it expected: Assignment type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Nothing' was expected.

With several type parameters, each star is projected on its own. Map<*, *> reads keys and values as Any?. A function type (Int) -> String is Function1<in P, out R>, so Function1<*, String> is Function1<in Nothing, String>. You can't call it, because no argument fits, but you know any result would be a String. Function1<Int, *> is the opposite: you can call it with an Int, and the result is Any?. The same reasoning rules out comparing through a Comparable<*>: Receiver type 'Comparable<*>' contains star projection which prohibits the use of 'fun compareTo(other: T): Int'.

The figure puts the three rules side by side.

sections.h: • is not Any?, and it is not a raw type
sections.html:
Two other types look like "a list of anything", and both differ from *.

MutableList<Any?> is a list whose element type is exactly Any?. You can add anything to it. But MutableList is invariant, so a MutableList<String> is not a MutableList<Any?>, and a function that takes one won't accept the other:

Java
static void addMarker(List<Object> list) { list.add("marker"); }
static int sizeOf(List<?> list) { return list.size(); }

addMarker(anything);   // a List<Object>: fine
sizeOf(ids);           // a List<String>: fine
addMarker(ids);        // error: List<String> cannot be converted to List<Object>
Kotlin
fun addMarker(list: MutableList<Any?>) { list.add("marker") }
fun sizeOf(list: MutableList<*>): Int = list.size

addMarker(anything)    // a MutableList<Any?>: fine
sizeOf(ids)            // a MutableList<String>: fine
addMarker(ids)         // error: actual type is 'MutableList<String>', but 'MutableList<Any?>' was expected.

So choose by what the function does. If it adds arbitrary values, it needs a real MutableList<Any?> and can only take one. If it doesn't care about the element type, it takes MutableList<*> and accepts every mutable list. For read-only List the difference disappears: List is covariant, so List<Any?> and List<*> accept the same arguments.

Java has a third option that Kotlin doesn't: the raw type. A raw List, with no angle brackets at all, switches generic checking off. It exists so that code written before Java 5 added generics still compiles:

Java
@SuppressWarnings({"rawtypes", "unchecked"})
static void addRaw(List list) { list.add(42); }

addRaw(ids);                 // compiles: an Integer goes into a List<String>
String last = ids.get(1);    // ClassCastException here, far from the bug
Kotlin
// Kotlin has no raw types. A Java raw List arrives in Kotlin as List<*>,
// so the same write is refused at compile time:
fun addRaw(list: MutableList<*>) { list.add(42) }   // error: ... prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'

The Kotlin docs say star projections are "very much like Java's raw types, but safe". In Java, write List<?> instead of a raw List whenever you mean "I don't know the type". It reads the same and keeps the checks on.

sections.h: Type checks need a star, then you check each element
sections.html:
JSON libraries, message headers and old Java APIs hand you values typed Any? or Map<*, *>. To use them, you check what they are. The first check most people write doesn't compile:

if (amounts is List<Long>) println("a list of longs")
Cannot check for instance of erased type 'List<Long>'.

At run time a List<Long> and a List<String> are the same kind of ArrayList object, so the JVM can check the class and nothing more. Lesson 8 of this track explains erasure in full. For now the rule is: check with a star, then check each element you use.

Java
static List<Long> amountsIn(Object payload) {
    List<Long> out = new ArrayList<>();
    if (payload instanceof List<?> list) {
        for (Object e : list) if (e instanceof Long l) out.add(l);   // check every element
    }
    return out;
}
Kotlin
fun amountsIn(payload: Any?): List<Long> {
    if (payload !is List<*>) return emptyList()
    return payload.mapNotNull { it as? Long }     // payload is now a List<*>; check each element
}

After the !is List<*> line returns early, the compiler smart-casts payload to List<*> for the rest of the function. A when with is List<*> and is Map<*, *> branches does the same in each branch. Java's instanceof List<?> list (pattern matching for instanceof, final since Java 16) gives you the same kind of typed variable. Java's error for the bad check is Object cannot be safely cast to List<Long>.

One full check does compile: when the compiler already knows the type argument. With c: Collection<String>, c is List<String> is fine, because only the class part needs checking at run time.

The shortcut to avoid is payload as List<Long>. It compiles with an unchecked-cast warning and succeeds for any list at all. The ClassCastException comes later, at whichever line first reads a String as a Long. Checking the elements costs one line and fails in the right place.

Better still, avoid the untyped route when you can. Ask the JSON library to bind the body to a data class, and the checking happens once, inside the library. Lesson 9 of this track shows how type tokens make that work for generic targets such as List<Settlement>.

try.expect: Both print object with keys [id, amounts], array of 3, value 42 and amounts = [1200, 350]: the stray string is skipped. The wrong move fails with Cannot check for instance of erased type 'List<Long>'. (Java: Object cannot be safely cast to List<Long>). With as Long, the run fails with ClassCastException: class java.lang.String cannot be cast to class java.lang.Long inside amountsIn, far from wherever the payload was built.

analogy: A star-projected list is a sealed shipping container whose manifest has been torn off. You know it holds one kind of goods, you just don't know which. You may unload items and handle each one as "some item", you may count them, and you may empty the container. You may not load anything in, because you can't know whether it matches what's inside. MutableList<Any?> is a different container, one labeled "mixed goods", which takes anything; a container of bananas is not a mixed-goods container, even though bananas are goods. The analogy breaks at the dock: a worker could open a box and read the label on the goods, but the JVM cannot recover a list's element type at run time at all. That is why is List<String> isn't allowed.
world: Star projections are the honest type for data whose shape you only learn at run time. A webhook from a card issuer parsed with objectMapper.readValue(body, Map::class.java) comes back as a Map<*, *>, because Map::class.java is a Class<Map<*, *>>. Kafka record headers, Temporal payload converters and Quarkus config maps all hand you values of unknown element type. Log them with Map<*, *> and List<*>, check shapes with is Map<*, *>, and pull out typed values element by element with as?. A metrics helper that reports the size of any in-memory buffer takes a Collection<*>. On the Java side of the codebase, replace raw List and Map parameters with List<?> and Map<?, ?>.
mistake: The common mistake is writing Any? when you mean "unknown": fun logAll(items: MutableList<Any?>) or fun audit(fields: Map<Any?, Any?>). It looks maximally general, but MutableList and Map's key are invariant, so a caller's MutableList<String> or Map<String, Int> is rejected, and the caller ends up copying or casting to fit. The Java version of the same reflex is a raw List parameter, which compiles for everyone and silently turns checking off. The fix is to say what you mean: MutableList<*> / Map<*, *> in Kotlin and List<?> / Map<?, ?> in Java when you don't care about the type, and a real MutableList<Any?> only when you genuinely store arbitrary values.

compare.title: Unknown type arguments: Kotlin's * and Java's ?

java.title: Payloads.java
java.html: import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.stream.Collectors; final class Payloads { static String describe(Object value) { if (value == null) return "nothing"; if (value instanceof String s) return "text " + s; if (value instanceof List<?> l) return "list of " + l.size(); // List<String> would not compile if (value instanceof Map<?, ?> m) return "map of " + m.size(); return "other"; } static String render(Map<?, ?> map) { // keys and values are Object return map.entrySet().stream() .sorted((a, b) -> String.valueOf(a.getKey()).compareTo(String.valueOf(b.getKey()))) .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + (e.getValue() instanceof Map<?, ?> m ? render(m) : e.getValue())) .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "{", "}")); } static int drain(List<?> buffer) { // not a raw List: checks stay on int n = buffer.size(); buffer.clear(); return n; } }

kotlin.title: Payloads.kt
kotlin.html: fun describe(value: Any?): String = when (value) { null -> "nothing" is String -> "text $value" is List<*> -> "list of ${value.size}" // List<String> would not compile is Map<*, *> -> "map of ${value.size}" else -> "other" } fun render(map: Map<*, *>): String = // keys and values are Any? map.entries .sortedBy { it.key.toString() } .joinToString(", ", "{", "}") { (k, v) -> "$k=${if (v is Map<*, *>) render(v) else v}" } fun drain(buffer: MutableList<*>): Int { // Kotlin has no raw types val n = buffer.size buffer.clear() return n }

compare.note: Kotlin's MutableList<*> compiles to Java's List<?>, and the two behave almost the same: reads give Any? / Object, writes of real values are refused, and members that take no element still work. Three things differ. Java lets you pass null through a ?; Kotlin refuses, because the unknown type might be non-nullable. Java still has raw types, which switch checking off; Kotlin has none, and shows a Java raw List as List<*>. And Kotlin works out what * means from the declaration's variance, so a star on an in parameter becomes in Nothing and a star on an out T : Number keeps the Number bound, while Java applies the same capture rules to every wildcard.

worked.title: Render an untyped webhook payload for the audit log

steps.say: A card issuer's webhook is parsed into a map whose types you don't control. The first draft of the audit renderer asks for Map<Any?, Any?> to be "as general as possible". The parsed map in a test is a Map<String, Int>. Read the error.
steps.code: fun render(map: Map<Any?, Any?>): String = map.toString() val webhook: Map<String, Int> = mapOf("cents" to 1_200) render(webhook) // error: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Map<String, Int>', but 'Map<Any?, Any?>' was expected.

alt.html: static String render(Map<Object, Object> map) { return map.toString(); } Map<String, Integer> webhook = Map.of("cents", 1_200); render(webhook); // error: incompatible types: Map<String,Integer> cannot be converted to Map<Object,Object>

steps.say: Map<K, out V> is covariant in V but invariant in K, so Map<String, Int> is not a Map<Any?, Any?>. The renderer never puts anything into the map; it only reads. So it doesn't need to name either type. Use one star per type parameter.
steps.code: fun render(map: Map<*, *>): String = map.entries .sortedBy { it.key.toString() } // 1. keys are Any?: toString() works, even on null .joinToString(", ", "{", "}") { (k, v) -> "$k=$v" }

alt.html: static String render(Map<?, ?> map) { return map.entrySet().stream() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(e -> String.valueOf(e.getKey()))) // 1. keys are Object .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue()) .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "{", "}")); }

steps.say: Payloads nest: the card field is itself a map. Check the value's shape with a star, and the smart cast gives you a Map<*, *> to recurse on. Self-check before reading the comment: why not v is Map<String, Any?>? (Type arguments are erased, so the compiler refuses that check.)
steps.code: fun render(map: Map<*, *>): String = map.entries .sortedBy { it.key.toString() } .joinToString(", ", "{", "}") { (k, v) -> val shown = if (v is Map<*, *>) render(v) else v.toString() // 2. smart cast to Map<*, *> "$k=$shown" } render(mapOf("cents" to 99, "card" to mapOf("scheme" to "visa", "last4" to "4242"))) // {card={last4=4242, scheme=visa}, cents=99}

alt.html: static String render(Map<?, ?> map) { return map.entrySet().stream() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(e -> String.valueOf(e.getKey()))) .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + (e.getValue() instanceof Map<?, ?> m ? render(m) : e.getValue())) // 2. pattern match .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "{", "}")); }

steps.say: Now any map fits: Map<String, Int>, Map<String, Any?>, the Map<*, *> that a JSON library returns, or a map with Int keys. The renderer is honest about what it knows. This is the render function in the lab, and the tests check exactly this output.

lab.title: Describe, render and drain values of unknown type
steps: Run the tests. All nine fail. The two signature tests show what Java sees today: but was: "List<Object>" for drain and but was: "List" (a raw type) for countNulls.
In Describe.kt, write describe as one when (value) with the branches in the order the KDoc lists them.
Write stringsIn: return early unless value is List<*>, then keep the elements that are Strings.
Fix drain's parameter type so any mutable list fits, then clear it and return the old size.
In MapPrinter.kt, write render. Sort the entries by key.toString() and recurse into values that are Map<*, *>.
In Nulls.java, change the raw List to List<?>, remove the @SuppressWarnings, and count the nulls. Run until all nine pass.
hints: when (value) { null -> ...; is String -> ...; is List<*> -> ...; is Map<*, *> -> ...; is Number -> ...; else -> ... }. Each branch smart-casts value.
In stringsIn, for (e in value) if (e is String) out += e: each element is Any? until you check it.
Why does drain need * and not Any?? MutableList<Any?> is invariant, so it only accepts lists whose element type is exactly Any?.

drill.title: What does each star allow?
drill.prompt: Close this page. Declare interface Source<out T : Number> { fun next(): T }, interface Sink<in T> { fun accept(item: T) } and class Box<T>(var item: T). Write one function that takes a Source<*>, a Sink<*>, a Box<*> and a MutableList<*>, and does the one legal thing with each. In a comment, say what each star stands for. Then write the Java version, which has one extra legal call.

answer.html: interface Source<out T : Number> { fun next(): T } interface Sink<in T> { fun accept(item: T) } class Box<T>(var item: T) fun drill(s: Source<*>, k: Sink<*>, b: Box<*>, l: MutableList<*>) { val n: Number = s.next() // Source<*> = Source<out Number>: reads keep the bound // k.accept(...) // Sink<*> = Sink<in Nothing>: nothing can be passed in val i: Any? = b.item // Box<*> reads as Box<out Any?> (and writes as Box<in Nothing>) l.clear() // MutableList<*>: members that take no element still work }

alt.title: Drill.java
alt.html: interface Source<T extends Number> { T next(); } interface Sink<T> { void accept(T item); } class Box<T> { T item; } static void drill(Source<?> s, Sink<?> k, Box<?> b, List<?> l) { Number n = s.next(); // the bound survives the ? k.accept(null); // the extra legal call: Java lets null through a ? Object i = b.item; // reads as Object l.clear(); // takes no element }

recap: List<*> means a list of one specific element type that you don't know. Reads give Any?; Java writes it List<?>.
Through a star projection you can't pass an element in. Kotlin refuses even null; Java allows null.
* becomes the safest projection: out Bound for an out parameter, in Nothing for an in parameter, both for an invariant one.
MutableList<Any?> is a list of exactly Any? and rejects a MutableList<String>. MutableList<*> accepts every mutable list.
Java's raw types switch checking off. Kotlin has none and shows a Java raw List as List<*>.
Check unknown values with is List<*> or is Map<*, *>, then check each element with is or as?.

explain.prompt: A teammate wrote fun logFields(fields: Map<Any?, Any?>) and now every caller with a Map<String, Int> has a type error. They ask whether Map<*, *> is just a shorter way to write Map<Any?, Any?>. Explain the difference in your own words.
explain.answer: Map<Any?, Any?> is one specific type: a map whose keys and values are declared as Any?. Because Map is invariant in its key type, a Map<String, Int> is not that type, so callers get an error. Map<*, *> means "a map of some key type and some value type that I don't know". Every map fits it. In exchange, the function can only do things that are safe for any key and value type: read keys and values as Any?, ask for the size, iterate. It can't call methods that take a key or value of the unknown type in a way that would store one. A logging function only reads, so Map<*, *> is the honest type. Map<Any?, Any?> only makes sense if you build a map that really holds arbitrary keys and values.

deeper.html:
Kotlin can still call a generic function with a star-projected argument. Given fun <T> swap(l: MutableList<T>, i: Int, j: Int), the call swap(star, 0, 1) with star: MutableList<*> compiles with kotlinc 2.4.21 and swaps the two elements. The compiler captures the unknown element type as T for that one call, so inside swap a value read from the list may be written back into the same list. Java does the same with a private helper method, the "capture helper" pattern; the JDK's Collections.swap(List<?> list, int i, int j) skips it and uses a raw type under @SuppressWarnings.

The Map interface has a detail worth knowing. It is declared Map<K, out V>, invariant in K. So on a Map<*, *> the member get(key: K) would take in Nothing, and you could never look anything up. The standard library adds an extension, Map<out K, V>.get(key: K), so payload["amounts"] on a Map<*, *> still compiles and returns Any?.

Stars also appear in class literals: Map::class.java is a Class<Map<*, *>>, and listOf(1)::class is a KClass<out List<Int>>. The class object of a generic class exists once for all type arguments, so it can't carry them. Lesson 9 of this track is about exactly that. And in Kotlin's own reflection, typeOf<List<*>>().arguments prints [*]: the star is part of the type, not an absence of one.
